stimulus: Office manager: An internal review found that employees who regularly eat lunch away from their desks make fewer errors in the afternoon than employees who eat at their desks. Therefore, requiring all employees to take their lunch breaks away from their desks would reduce the number of afternoon errors made in this office.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: fails to consider that errors made in the morning may be at least as costly to the office as errors made in the afternoon
choices.B: relies on an internal review rather than on a study conducted by independent researchers
choices.C: overlooks the possibility that employees who make fewer errors are the ones who choose to eat away from their desks
choices.D: presumes that eating lunch away from one's desk is the only way to reduce afternoon errors
choices.E: generalizes from the employees of one office to employees in general

explanations.A: Out of scope: the conclusion concerns only 'afternoon errors,' so the cost of morning errors has no bearing on whether the inference holds.
explanations.B: Wrong force: who conducted the review is a quibble about the data; even an independent study showing the same correlation would leave the causal leap unsupported.
explanations.C: Correct. The review shows only a correlation. Careful, low-error employees may simply be the ones who choose to leave their desks, in which case forcing everyone out would change nothing. The argument assumes the direction of causation.
explanations.D: Extreme: the manager says the requirement 'would reduce' errors, not that it is the 'only way' to do so; the argument never needs that claim.
explanations.E: Wrong part: the conclusion is explicitly about 'this office,' so no generalization to 'employees in general' is made.

keyTakeaway: When a correlation becomes a mandate, ask whether the people who already have the good outcome are the ones choosing the behavior.
predictionHint: Correlation to cause: low-error employees may self-select into eating away from their desks.

stimulus: Newspaper editor: Over the past month, our paper has received more than three hundred letters concerning the proposed downtown stadium, and nearly nine out of ten of them oppose the project. Our readership is drawn from every neighborhood in the city. It is clear, therefore, that the great majority of this city's residents oppose the stadium.
stem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: assumes that residents who oppose the stadium will vote against the officials who support it
choices.B: bases a conclusion about the city's residents on the views of people who chose to write letters, who may not be typical
choices.C: fails to consider that the newspaper's readers may not be distributed equally across every neighborhood of the city
choices.D: overlooks the possibility that a substantial number of the letters opposing the stadium were written by the same few individuals
choices.E: treats the fact that most residents oppose the stadium as showing that the stadium should not be built

explanations.A: Out of scope: the conclusion is about what residents think, not about how they will 'vote.'
explanations.B: Correct. People who take the trouble to write letters are self-selected and tend to be those with strong feelings, usually opposition. Three hundred letter writers tell us little about 'the great majority of this city's residents.'
explanations.C: Shell game: this swaps the real problem (self-selection of letter writers) for an unevenness in readership that the premise 'drawn from every neighborhood' already addresses and that would not fix the inference anyway.
explanations.D: Wrong force: even if every letter came from a different person, three hundred self-selected writers would still not represent the city, so this is not the argument's central weakness.
explanations.E: Wrong part: the editor concludes only that residents 'oppose the stadium,' not that it 'should not be built.'

keyTakeaway: People who volunteer their opinions are a self-selected sample; the silent majority may feel differently.
predictionHint: Letter writers are not a representative sample of residents.

stimulus: Music director: Every musician in the newly formed Castellan Chamber Orchestra was selected from among the finest players in the region, and each has an outstanding record as a soloist. The orchestra's first concert is therefore certain to be an outstanding performance.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument's reasoning?

choices.A: It presumes that an orchestra made up of excellent soloists will perform excellently as a group.
choices.B: It takes for granted that the musicians were selected by a fair and impartial process.
choices.C: It fails to consider that audiences may judge a performance by standards other than technical excellence.
choices.D: It infers that because the musicians have performed well in the past, each will perform well in the first concert.
choices.E: It relies on the opinion of the music director, who has an interest in the orchestra's success.

explanations.A: Correct. Playing well together requires balance, blend, and ensemble rehearsal, none of which follows from each member's excellence 'as a soloist.' The argument moves from a property of each part to a property of the whole.
explanations.B: Out of scope: how the players were chosen does not matter; the premise grants that they are the finest, and the gap remains.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: the conclusion is about whether the performance will be 'outstanding,' and nothing in the argument turns on how audiences judge it.
explanations.D: Shell game: the problem is not projecting each individual's past success into the future but assuming that individual success translates into group success.
explanations.E: Out of scope: the director's interest does not identify an error in the reasoning offered; the premises are granted as true.

keyTakeaway: Excellence of each member does not guarantee excellence of the group when the group's performance depends on how the members work together.
predictionHint: Composition: great soloists do not automatically make a great ensemble.

stimulus: Every medication that the national health agency has approved for sale has passed a full series of safety trials. Dorelin, a new medication for treating migraines, has just passed a full series of safety trials. Therefore, Dorelin has been approved by the agency for sale.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: fails to consider that medications may be approved for sale by agencies in other countries
choices.B: takes for granted that the safety trials Dorelin passed were as rigorous as those required by the agency
choices.C: treats a condition that all approved medications satisfy as though satisfying it guaranteed approval
choices.D: overlooks the possibility that Dorelin may not be effective in treating migraines
choices.E: presumes that a medication that has passed safety trials is safe for all patients

explanations.A: Out of scope: the conclusion concerns approval by 'the agency,' so what other countries do is irrelevant.
explanations.B: Shell game: both premises speak of 'a full series of safety trials,' so rigor is not where the argument breaks; even identical trials would not entail approval.
explanations.C: Correct. 'Every approved medication has passed trials' makes passing trials necessary for approval, not sufficient. Dorelin could have passed and still await, or be denied, approval.
explanations.D: True but irrelevant: effectiveness is never at issue; the conclusion is about whether approval 'has been' granted.
explanations.E: Extreme: the argument makes no claim that Dorelin is 'safe for all patients'; it concludes only that it has been approved.

keyTakeaway: 'All A are B' never licenses 'this B is an A'; satisfying a necessary condition does not establish the outcome.
predictionHint: Mistaken reversal: passing trials is required for approval, not a guarantee of it.

stimulus: Radio host: A prominent nutritionist recently published a book urging people to reduce the amount of refined sugar in their diets, citing studies linking high sugar intake to several chronic diseases. Yet the nutritionist was photographed last week enjoying an elaborate dessert at a restaurant. Readers should therefore disregard her advice about reducing their sugar intake.
stem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: relies on a single photograph as evidence of the nutritionist's habitual eating patterns
choices.B: rejects a recommendation on the grounds that the person making it does not appear to follow it
choices.C: assumes that the studies the nutritionist cited were conducted by the nutritionist herself
choices.D: fails to consider that eating an occasional dessert may be entirely compatible with a diet that is low in refined sugar
choices.E: treats the popularity of the nutritionist's book as evidence that its advice is unsound

explanations.A: Shell game: even if the nutritionist ate dessert every night, her own habits would say nothing about whether the studies she cites support her advice.
explanations.B: Correct. The host attacks the advisor's conduct rather than the advice, which rests on 'studies linking high sugar intake to several chronic diseases.' Whether she practices what she preaches is beside the point.
explanations.C: Out of scope: nothing in the argument depends on who conducted the studies.
explanations.D: Half right: this is a fair observation, but it concedes the host's framing. Even if the dessert were inconsistent with her advice, the advice would still stand or fall on the evidence.
explanations.E: Wrong part: the book's popularity is never mentioned, let alone used as a reason to reject the advice.

keyTakeaway: An advisor's failure to follow her own advice is a fact about the advisor, not a defect in the advice.
predictionHint: Ad hominem: the dessert says nothing about the studies.

stimulus: Advertisement: Some physicians have expressed concern about Tranquilex, an herbal sleep remedy. But Tranquilex has been sold in this country for over fifteen years, and in all that time not one scientific study has demonstrated that it causes any harm. Consumers can therefore be confident that Tranquilex is completely safe.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument's reasoning?

choices.A: It treats the absence of evidence that a product is harmful as proof that the product is safe.
choices.B: It fails to consider that Tranquilex may be less effective than other sleep remedies.
choices.C: It assumes that physicians' concerns about a product are motivated by hostility toward herbal remedies.
choices.D: It overlooks the fact that a product can be sold for many years without being popular.
choices.E: It infers that a product is safe merely because government regulators have permitted it to be sold for a long time.

explanations.A: Correct. 'Not one study has demonstrated' harm is compatible with no one having studied the remedy at all. Lack of evidence of harm is not evidence of safety, let alone of being 'completely safe.'
explanations.B: Out of scope: effectiveness is never at issue; the conclusion concerns safety.
explanations.C: Out of scope: the advertisement says nothing about why physicians are concerned.
explanations.D: True but irrelevant: popularity plays no role in the argument, which relies on the absence of studies showing harm.
explanations.E: Shell game: regulators are never mentioned; the premise is that the product 'has been sold,' not that it has been approved.

keyTakeaway: 'No study has shown X' supports only 'X has not been shown,' never 'not-X is true.'
predictionHint: Absence of evidence of harm is treated as proof of safety.

stimulus: Business reporter: Last year, sales of electric scooters made by Vantor rose by 60 percent, while sales of scooters made by its rival Brightline rose by only 8 percent. So Vantor must now sell more electric scooters each year than Brightline does.
stem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: fails to establish that the two companies' sales were measured over the same period
choices.B: overlooks the possibility that a percentage increase in sales can be large even when the starting number of sales is small
choices.C: takes for granted that the growth in Vantor's sales will continue at the same rate in future years as it did last year
choices.D: confuses the number of scooters sold with the revenue earned from those sales
choices.E: assumes that Brightline's lower growth rate was caused by Vantor's higher growth rate

explanations.A: Premise booster: the stimulus says both figures are for 'last year,' so the period is already fixed.
explanations.B: Correct. A 60 percent rise from 1,000 scooters is 600 units; an 8 percent rise from 100,000 is 8,000. Growth rates say nothing about absolute totals, so Vantor may still sell far fewer scooters.
explanations.C: Wrong part: the conclusion is about what Vantor sells 'now,' not about future growth.
explanations.D: Shell game: the argument speaks consistently of 'sales' as units sold; revenue never enters.
explanations.E: Out of scope: no causal relationship between the two companies' growth rates is asserted or needed.

keyTakeaway: A percentage change tells you nothing about absolute size without the base it was computed from.
predictionHint: Percent versus number: a big percentage rise from a small base can still be a small total.

stimulus: Commentator: Everyone agrees that in a free society people have a right to hold and express whatever opinions they wish. A newspaper columnist who recently expressed the opinion that the city's new transit plan will fail was therefore right to do so, and her critics, who claim her judgment was mistaken, must themselves be in error.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: relies on the claim that everyone agrees with a principle in order to establish that the principle is correct
choices.B: fails to consider that the columnist might have had good reasons to believe the transit plan will fail
choices.C: trades on two different meanings of the word 'right'
choices.D: assumes that anyone who criticizes an opinion is thereby attempting to suppress the expression of that opinion
choices.E: treats the columnist's expertise on transit matters as sufficient to settle the question of the plan's prospects

explanations.A: Wrong part: even granting the principle outright, the conclusion would not follow; the failure lies in how 'right' is used, not in how the principle is supported.
explanations.B: Out of scope: whether the columnist had good reasons is irrelevant, since the argument never appeals to her reasons.
explanations.C: Correct. The premise concerns a 'right' in the sense of an entitlement to speak; the conclusion that she was 'right' and her critics 'in error' uses 'right' to mean correct. Having permission to say something does not make it true.
explanations.D: Shell game: the critics are described as claiming 'her judgment was mistaken,' not as trying to suppress her; the argument does not rely on this.
explanations.E: Out of scope: the columnist's expertise is never mentioned.

keyTakeaway: When a conclusion repeats a word from the premise, check that the word still means the same thing.
predictionHint: 'Right' as entitlement versus 'right' as correct.

stimulus: Medical researcher: In a study of patients recovering from knee surgery, those who scored high on a measure of optimism administered two weeks after surgery regained full mobility sooner than those who scored low. Since the optimistic patients recovered more quickly, optimism evidently speeds recovery, and surgeons should encourage knee-surgery patients to cultivate a positive outlook before their operations.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument's reasoning?

choices.A: It relies on a measure of optimism that may not accurately capture patients' actual outlook.
choices.B: It generalizes from patients recovering from knee surgery to patients recovering from all types of surgery.
choices.C: It overlooks the possibility that some patients who scored low on the optimism measure regained full mobility sooner than some who scored high.
choices.D: It fails to consider that patients who were already recovering well two weeks after surgery may for that reason have been more optimistic.
choices.E: It takes for granted that regaining full mobility is the only measure of recovery relevant to patients.

explanations.A: Wrong force: doubting the measure attacks the data rather than the inference; even a perfect measure of optimism would leave the direction of causation unsettled.
explanations.B: Wrong part: the recommendation is addressed to 'knee-surgery patients,' so no generalization to 'all types of surgery' is made.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: the finding is a group-level comparison, which tolerates individual exceptions.
explanations.D: Correct. Optimism was measured 'two weeks after surgery,' when some patients were already healing faster. Good early recovery could produce optimism rather than the reverse, so the recommendation to cultivate optimism beforehand is unsupported.
explanations.E: Extreme: the argument does not need mobility to be the 'only' relevant measure, just a reasonable one.

keyTakeaway: When the supposed cause is measured after the effect has begun, suspect that the arrow runs the other way.
predictionHint: Reverse causation: recovering well may make patients optimistic.

stimulus: Software executive: Before releasing the redesigned interface for our accounting application, we asked forty of our own engineers to complete a set of common tasks using it. All forty completed every task quickly and described the interface as intuitive. We can therefore expect that our customers, most of whom are small-business owners, will also find the redesigned interface intuitive.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: fails to consider that customers may be reluctant to adopt any new interface, however intuitive
choices.B: relies on the reports of participants who may have been reluctant to criticize a product developed by their own company
choices.C: draws a conclusion about a population from a sample whose members differ from that population in a relevant respect
choices.D: takes for granted that an interface that is intuitive is also one that enables users to complete tasks quickly
choices.E: presumes that forty participants constitute a sample large enough to support a generalization

explanations.A: Out of scope: the conclusion is that customers will 'find the interface intuitive,' not that they will adopt it.
explanations.B: Half right: bias in the engineers' self-reports is a real worry, but the argument also has objective evidence that they 'completed every task quickly.' The deeper problem is who the testers were, not what they said.
explanations.C: Correct. Software engineers, who build such tools for a living, are far more adept with interfaces than 'small-business owners.' That difference is exactly the one that matters for whether an interface feels intuitive.
explanations.D: Reversal: the argument uses quick completion as evidence of intuitiveness, not the other way around, and never needs this link.
explanations.E: Wrong force: the issue is not how many engineers were tested but that they were engineers; four hundred would not help.

keyTakeaway: A sample fails not only by being small but by differing from the target group in the very trait being measured.
predictionHint: Engineers are not representative of small-business owners when it comes to using software.

stimulus: Economist: Critics claim that the past decade of economic policy has failed ordinary citizens. But during that decade, the nation's total economic output grew by nearly 30 percent after adjusting for inflation. Since the nation as a whole became considerably wealthier, it follows that the typical household is considerably wealthier now than it was a decade ago.
stem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: assumes that growth in total economic output is the only legitimate measure of a policy's success
choices.B: fails to consider that inflation may have been higher during the decade than official figures indicate
choices.C: overlooks the possibility that the critics are concerned with matters other than household wealth
choices.D: treats a claim about a change in wealth over a decade as if it were a claim about current levels of wealth
choices.E: infers that what is true of a nation as a whole must be true of a typical member of that nation

explanations.A: Extreme: the economist uses output growth as evidence, not as the 'only legitimate measure' of anything.
explanations.B: Premise booster: the figure is stated to be 'after adjusting for inflation,' so this challenges a premise rather than the reasoning.
explanations.C: Out of scope: what the critics care about does not affect whether the inference from national output to household wealth is valid.
explanations.D: Shell game: both the premise and the conclusion compare wealth 'now' with a decade ago; no shift to 'current levels' occurs.
explanations.E: Correct. Total output can grow 30 percent while the gains accrue to a small share of households, leaving the 'typical household' no better off. An aggregate increase does not distribute itself evenly.

keyTakeaway: What is true of a total or an average need not be true of the typical member; distribution matters.
predictionHint: Division: national growth does not mean every household grew.

stimulus: Structural engineer: Any building that fully complies with the current seismic code will withstand a moderate earthquake without structural damage. The Harlan Street warehouse, built decades before the current code was adopted, does not fully comply with it. We must therefore conclude that the warehouse would suffer structural damage in a moderate earthquake.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument's reasoning?

choices.A: It takes for granted that buildings constructed before the current code was adopted cannot be brought into compliance with it.
choices.B: It treats a condition that guarantees a building's withstanding a moderate earthquake as a condition required for doing so.
choices.C: It fails to specify what distinguishes a moderate earthquake from a severe one.
choices.D: It overlooks the possibility that the warehouse would suffer structural damage in a severe earthquake.
choices.E: It assumes that a building that complies with the current code will withstand any earthquake, however severe.

explanations.A: Out of scope: whether the warehouse could be upgraded is irrelevant; the conclusion concerns its present condition.
explanations.B: Correct. Compliance is sufficient for withstanding a moderate quake, but nothing says it is necessary. A sturdy old building might survive without complying. Denying the sufficient condition tells us nothing.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: 'moderate' is used consistently in premise and conclusion, so vagueness does not create the gap.
explanations.D: Out of scope: the conclusion concerns a 'moderate' earthquake; what a severe one would do is beside the point.
explanations.E: Extreme: the premise is limited to 'a moderate earthquake'; the argument never extends it to 'any earthquake.'

keyTakeaway: From 'if A then B,' not-A tells you nothing about B; only not-B lets you infer not-A.
predictionHint: Mistaken negation: not complying does not mean not surviving.

stimulus: Letter to the editor: Our schools should not present the geological account of continental drift as established fact. Geologists themselves describe it as a theory, and a theory is, after all, merely a conjecture that has yet to be confirmed. Students deserve to be told that the movement of continents remains an unconfirmed speculation.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: assumes that students are incapable of evaluating scientific evidence for themselves
choices.B: equivocates between a technical use of the word 'theory' and its everyday use
choices.C: fails to consider that geologists may disagree among themselves about the details of continental drift
choices.D: treats the fact that an account has not been proven with certainty as showing that it is probably false
choices.E: presumes that whatever geologists say about their own discipline must be accurate

explanations.A: Out of scope: nothing in the argument concerns students' abilities.
explanations.B: Correct. When geologists call continental drift a 'theory,' they mean a well-supported explanatory framework. The letter substitutes the everyday sense, 'merely a conjecture,' and draws its conclusion from that switch.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: disagreement about details does not bear on whether the account as a whole is 'unconfirmed speculation.'
explanations.D: Shell game: the letter concludes that the account is 'unconfirmed,' not that it is 'probably false'; this misdescribes the conclusion.
explanations.E: Wrong part: the argument does rely on what geologists say, but its error is in misreading them, not in trusting them.

keyTakeaway: A word borrowed from experts may carry a technical meaning that the everyday sense does not share.
predictionHint: 'Theory' in science is not 'theory' as mere guess.

stimulus: Reviewer: Several historians have challenged the account of the causes of the Brennic War given in Alder's widely used textbook. Their challenge is misguided. Alder holds an endowed chair in history at one of the most respected universities in the country, and his textbook has been adopted by hundreds of schools. His account of the war's causes is therefore the correct one.
stem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: attacks the historians who challenge Alder's account rather than addressing the substance of their challenge
choices.B: presumes that a textbook adopted by hundreds of schools cannot contain any factual errors
choices.C: fails to consider that the causes of a war may be too complex to be adequately captured by any single historian's account
choices.D: treats the standing of the author and the popularity of the book as establishing the truth of a specific claim in the book
choices.E: assumes that historians who challenge an established account must have an ulterior motive

explanations.A: Shell game: the reviewer does not attack the challengers at all; the argument simply ignores their reasons and cites Alder's credentials.
explanations.B: Extreme: the reviewer need not assume the book is free of 'any' error, only that this account is correct; 'cannot contain any' overstates the assumption.
explanations.C: Out of scope: complexity of causes is a general observation that does not identify how the reviewer's inference fails.
explanations.D: Correct. An endowed chair and wide adoption are evidence of reputation, not of the accuracy of one contested claim. Credentials and popularity cannot settle a dispute among qualified historians about a specific question.
explanations.E: Out of scope: the reviewer says nothing about the challengers' motives.

keyTakeaway: Reputation and popularity are reasons to take a source seriously, not proof that any particular claim it makes is true.
predictionHint: Appeal to authority and popularity in place of evidence about the contested claim.

stimulus: Historian: The collapse of the Mirenian kingdom in the fifth century was brought about either by the incursions of neighboring peoples or by the decay of its own political institutions. Recently analyzed records show that the incursions of that period were sporadic raids that never threatened the kingdom's major cities. It follows that the decay of Mirenia's political institutions caused its collapse.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: relies on recently analyzed records whose accuracy regarding the scale of the incursions has not been independently verified
choices.B: fails to consider that sporadic raids, if sufficiently prolonged, could have weakened the kingdom's political institutions
choices.C: presumes, without justification, that the two causes it considers are the only ones that could have brought about the collapse
choices.D: takes for granted that a kingdom whose major cities are not threatened cannot collapse
choices.E: concludes that one explanation is correct merely because it has not been shown to be incorrect

explanations.A: Out of scope: doubts about the records attack a premise; the reasoning would still fail even if the records were perfectly accurate.
explanations.B: Half right: this interaction is possible, but it would still leave institutional decay as the proximate cause, so it does not undermine the conclusion.
explanations.C: Correct. The opening 'either...or' is asserted, not established. Plague, famine, climate, or economic collapse could have ended the kingdom. Eliminating one option forces the other only if the two really exhaust the possibilities.
explanations.D: Shell game: the argument uses the raids' limited scale to rule them out as the cause, not to claim the kingdom could not collapse.
explanations.E: Wrong part: the historian offers a positive argument by elimination, not a mere lack of refutation; this misdescribes the structure.

keyTakeaway: An argument by elimination is only as good as the claim that the listed options are the only options.
predictionHint: False dilemma: other causes of collapse are never ruled out.

stimulus: Columnist: Ten years ago, the city devoted 5 percent of its annual budget to the maintenance of public parks; this year it devotes only 3 percent. The city council's claim that it has not reduced park maintenance funding is thus plainly false.
stem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: overlooks the possibility that the total size of the city's budget has grown substantially over the decade
choices.B: presumes that maintaining public parks is a more important use of city funds than other uses
choices.C: fails to consider that the cost of maintaining parks may have risen over the decade
choices.D: confuses the percentage of the budget devoted to parks with the percentage of parks that are adequately maintained
choices.E: relies on figures from only two years rather than on figures from every year of the decade

explanations.A: Correct. If the budget doubled, 3 percent of it today exceeds 5 percent of it ten years ago. A falling share is compatible with rising funding, so the council's claim is not shown to be false.
explanations.B: Out of scope: the columnist makes a factual claim about funding, not a value claim about priorities.
explanations.C: Opposite: rising costs would mean the same dollars buy less maintenance, which would support the columnist's complaint rather than expose a flaw.
explanations.D: Shell game: the argument never mentions how well parks are maintained; both figures concern budget shares.
explanations.E: Wrong force: more years of data would not change the fact that a share is not an amount.

keyTakeaway: A smaller percentage of a larger total can be a larger amount; never read a share as an amount.
predictionHint: Percent of budget fell, but the budget itself may have grown.

stimulus: Activist: The newly enacted tax on home heating fuel is unjust. Any impartial observer who examined the tax without prejudice would recognize its unfairness. Those who have spoken in its defense have therefore shown that they are not impartial, and the views of partial observers carry no weight on questions of justice.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument's reasoning?

choices.A: It attacks the character of the tax's defenders instead of responding to the arguments they have offered.
choices.B: It fails to consider that a tax can be unfair to some people while being fair to the population as a whole.
choices.C: It takes for granted that the opinions of impartial observers are always correct on questions of justice.
choices.D: It generalizes from the views of a few defenders of the tax to the views of all who support it.
choices.E: It presupposes the truth of the claim that it is attempting to establish.

explanations.A: Half right: the activist does dismiss the defenders, but the dismissal is not a bare character attack; it is derived from the assumption that the tax is unfair, which is the deeper error.
explanations.B: Out of scope: the fair-to-some distinction has nothing to do with how the argument reaches its conclusion.
explanations.C: Premise booster: the argument states that impartial observers 'would recognize its unfairness,' so this is close to a stated premise, not a hidden gap.
explanations.D: Wrong part: the argument makes no claim about 'all who support' the tax; it concerns 'those who have spoken in its defense.'
explanations.E: Correct. The only way to know that the defenders are 'not impartial' is to already know that the tax is unfair, since their partiality is inferred from their failure to see that unfairness. The conclusion is assumed in order to discredit its opponents.

keyTakeaway: If the only evidence that opponents are biased is that they disagree with the conclusion, the argument is circular.
predictionHint: Disagreement is taken as proof of bias, which assumes the conclusion.

stimulus: Council member: The proposal to extend the tram line to the eastern districts was first put forward three years ago by Councillor Dray, who has since been convicted of accepting bribes in connection with an unrelated contract. A proposal that originated with someone so demonstrably corrupt should be rejected, and the council should therefore vote against the extension.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: fails to consider that extending the tram line to the eastern districts might cost more than alternative transportation projects would
choices.B: assumes that Councillor Dray's conviction was justified
choices.C: rejects a proposal on the basis of the character of its originator rather than on the basis of its merits
choices.D: overlooks the possibility that Councillor Dray accepted bribes in connection with the tram proposal as well
choices.E: treats the fact that a proposal was made three years ago as a reason to doubt its current relevance

explanations.A: Out of scope: the council member never discusses cost; the argument's only reason is Dray's corruption.
explanations.B: Premise booster: the stimulus states as fact that Dray 'has since been convicted,' so this challenges a premise rather than the inference.
explanations.C: Correct. The bribery concerned 'an unrelated contract,' and nothing about the extension's costs, benefits, or feasibility is discussed. Who proposed a plan has no bearing on whether it is a good plan.
explanations.D: Opposite: if true, this would give the council member a somewhat better reason for suspicion, so it describes no flaw.
explanations.E: Wrong part: the three-year gap is background; the argument does not use the passage of time as a reason.

keyTakeaway: The origin of a proposal, however disreputable, is not evidence about the proposal's merits.
predictionHint: Genetic fallacy: the proposer's corruption is not a reason against the proposal.

stimulus: Marketing director: In a survey of a representative sample of our customers, 68 percent said they would be willing to pay at least 20 percent more for clothing that is certified as sustainably produced. We should therefore introduce a line of certified sustainable clothing priced 20 percent above our standard line, confident that roughly two-thirds of our customers will buy it.
stem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: assumes that the sample of customers surveyed was representative of the company's customers as a whole
choices.B: fails to consider that certification as sustainably produced may itself add to the cost of producing the clothing
choices.C: overlooks the possibility that some customers would be willing to pay even more than 20 percent extra
choices.D: takes for granted that customers who say they would pay more for a product will actually do so
choices.E: presumes that customers who are unwilling to pay more for sustainable clothing would not buy it at the standard price

explanations.A: Premise booster: the stimulus stipulates 'a representative sample,' so representativeness is given, not assumed.
explanations.B: Out of scope: production cost bears on profit, not on the conclusion that two-thirds of customers 'will buy it.'
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: customers willing to pay even more would still be buyers; this does not threaten the prediction.
explanations.D: Correct. A stated willingness in a survey is a report of attitude, not a purchase. People routinely say they would pay more for ethical goods and then do not, so 'roughly two-thirds will buy' does not follow.
explanations.E: Out of scope: the conclusion is about who will buy the sustainable line; what the unwilling third would do is never at issue.

keyTakeaway: Survey responses report what people say they would do; behavior must be inferred separately.
predictionHint: Saying one would pay more is not the same as paying more.

stimulus: Anesthesiologist: The newly developed anesthetic Somnarol produces significantly fewer side effects than the anesthetic that has been standard for the past two decades, and it has been approved for use in all the procedures for which the standard anesthetic is used. Patients scheduled for surgery under Somnarol therefore have no reason to be concerned about side effects.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: takes for granted that patients' concerns about anesthesia are limited to concerns about side effects
choices.B: fails to consider that the standard anesthetic may have been improved during the past two decades
choices.C: presumes that an anesthetic approved for use in a procedure is appropriate for every patient who undergoes that procedure
choices.D: relies on the testimony of an anesthesiologist who may have a professional interest in the adoption of new anesthetics
choices.E: infers that something is good in some respect from the fact that it is better than an alternative in that respect

explanations.A: Out of scope: the conclusion is explicitly limited to concern 'about side effects,' so other concerns are not at issue.
explanations.B: True but irrelevant: whatever the standard anesthetic's history, the comparison is with it as it now is, and the gap would remain.
explanations.C: Shell game: approval is background in the argument; the inference to 'no reason to be concerned' rests on the comparison of side effects, not on approval.
explanations.D: Out of scope: the speaker's interests do not bear on whether the stated premises support the conclusion.
explanations.E: Correct. 'Fewer side effects than the standard' is a relative claim. If the standard anesthetic has many serious side effects, Somnarol could still have plenty, so 'no reason to be concerned' does not follow.

keyTakeaway: 'Better than X' is relative; it never establishes 'good' or 'safe' in absolute terms.
predictionHint: Fewer side effects than the standard does not mean no side effects worth worrying about.

stimulus: Physician: Prolonged psychological stress is known to produce insomnia in otherwise healthy adults, and the effect has been documented across many populations. My patient Oyelaran, who has no diagnosed physical illness, has suffered from persistent insomnia for the past several months. The most reasonable conclusion is that Oyelaran has been experiencing prolonged psychological stress, and the appropriate course is to treat that stress rather than the insomnia itself.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: infers that a particular factor is responsible for an effect merely from the fact that the factor is capable of producing that effect
choices.B: treats a condition that must be present for an effect to occur as though it were by itself sufficient to produce that effect
choices.C: presumes that insomnia cannot be caused by a physical illness that has not yet been diagnosed
choices.D: relies on evidence drawn from many populations to draw a conclusion about a single individual
choices.E: fails to consider that treating the insomnia directly might also alleviate the patient's stress

explanations.A: Correct. The premise establishes that stress can cause insomnia, not that insomnia is caused only by stress. Caffeine, noise, medication, or an undiagnosed condition could be responsible, so 'stress' is not 'the most reasonable conclusion' without ruling them out.
explanations.B: Reversal: the premise makes stress sufficient for insomnia, and the error is treating it as if it were necessary. This choice describes the mirror-image mistake and gets the direction wrong.
explanations.C: Half right: an undiagnosed illness is one overlooked alternative, but even if every physical illness were excluded, the inference would still ignore other causes. The flaw is more general than this.
explanations.D: Shell game: applying a well-documented general effect to an individual is not itself an error; the problem is which direction the inference runs.
explanations.E: Out of scope: the treatment recommendation is downstream of the diagnosis, and this does not address how the diagnosis was reached.

keyTakeaway: 'X can cause Y' does not license 'Y, therefore X'; a sufficient cause is not the only cause.
predictionHint: Stress is sufficient for insomnia, not necessary; the argument treats it as necessary.

stimulus: Business historian: I examined every manufacturing firm in the region that has remained in continuous operation for at least seventy-five years and found that each of them, throughout its history, kept its borrowing well below the industry average. Clearly, keeping borrowing low is what enables a manufacturing firm to survive over the long term, and firms in the region seeking longevity should adopt the same policy.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument's reasoning?

choices.A: It generalizes from manufacturing firms in one region to manufacturing firms in all regions.
choices.B: It overlooks the possibility that the industry average level of borrowing has changed considerably over seventy-five years.
choices.C: It takes for granted that what has enabled firms to survive in the past will enable firms to survive in the future.
choices.D: It fails to consider that low borrowing may be a consequence of a firm's long-term survival rather than its cause.
choices.E: It draws a causal conclusion without considering cases in which the supposed cause was present but the effect did not occur.

explanations.A: Wrong part: the recommendation is addressed to 'firms in the region,' so no generalization to 'all regions' is made.
explanations.B: True but irrelevant: 'throughout its history' already measures each firm against the average of its own time, so changes in the average do not disturb the premise.
explanations.C: Half right: the past-to-future assumption is a secondary gap in the recommendation, but the causal claim itself is unsupported before any projection into the future is made.
explanations.D: Reversal: the premise says borrowing was low 'throughout its history,' including before longevity was achieved, so survival cannot have caused the low borrowing.
explanations.E: Correct. The historian looked only at survivors. If many low-borrowing firms also went out of business, low borrowing would be no explanation of longevity at all. Without the failed firms, the sample cannot support a causal conclusion.

keyTakeaway: A trait shared by all the winners proves nothing unless you also know how many losers shared it.
predictionHint: Survivorship: where are the low-borrowing firms that failed?

stimulus: Hospital administrator: The consulting firm has proposed fourteen separate cost-saving measures, ranging from reducing the frequency of linen changes to consolidating two outpatient clinics. Our clinical staff reviewed each measure and concluded that none of them, taken by itself, would have any appreciable effect on the quality of patient care. We can therefore adopt all fourteen measures without any appreciable effect on the quality of patient care.
stem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: relies on the judgment of clinical staff members, who may lack the expertise needed to assess the financial consequences of the measures
choices.B: infers that a set of changes will have a certain property from the fact that each change considered individually has that property
choices.C: fails to consider that measures with no effect on patient care may nevertheless be unpopular with patients
choices.D: presumes that measures that do not affect the quality of patient care will produce significant cost savings
choices.E: overlooks the possibility that some of the fourteen measures would, taken individually, have an appreciable effect on patient care

explanations.A: Out of scope: the staff assessed effects on 'patient care,' not finances, so financial expertise is beside the point.
explanations.B: Correct. Fourteen individually negligible reductions can add up to a substantial one, and measures can interact. 'None by itself' does not establish 'all together,' which is the composition error.
explanations.C: Out of scope: popularity is never at issue; the conclusion concerns the 'quality of patient care.'
explanations.D: Shell game: the conclusion is about patient care, not about whether the measures will save money.
explanations.E: Premise booster: the stimulus states that staff found 'none of them, taken by itself' would have an effect; this simply denies a premise.

keyTakeaway: Effects that are negligible one at a time can be large in combination; 'each' does not imply 'all.'
predictionHint: Composition: fourteen small cuts can add up.

stimulus: Civil engineer: Unless the river levee is raised by at least two meters before the next major storm season, the low-lying districts of Marlow will be flooded. The regional authority has now approved funding to raise the levee by two and a half meters, and the work will be completed well before the storm season begins. The residents of the low-lying districts can therefore rest assured that their neighborhoods will not be flooded.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: takes for granted that the approved funding will be sufficient to complete the work as planned
choices.B: fails to consider that raising the levee may increase the risk of flooding in districts downstream of Marlow
choices.C: presumes that the low-lying districts are the only parts of Marlow at risk of flooding
choices.D: treats a measure whose omission would ensure an outcome as a measure whose adoption will prevent that outcome
choices.E: relies on a prediction about the severity of future storms that cannot be known in advance

explanations.A: Premise booster: the stimulus states that 'the work will be completed,' so adequacy of funding is given.
explanations.B: Out of scope: the conclusion concerns 'the low-lying districts of Marlow,' not districts downstream.
explanations.C: Extreme: the argument says nothing about other parts of Marlow and does not need them to be safe.
explanations.D: Correct. 'Unless raised, flooded' means that failing to raise the levee guarantees flooding. It does not say that raising the levee guarantees no flooding; the districts could flood from storm drains or a breach elsewhere. Necessary is treated as sufficient.
explanations.E: Wrong force: the engineer makes no prediction about storm severity; the premise is conditional on a 'major storm season,' whatever its severity.

keyTakeaway: 'Unless A, B' makes A necessary to avoid B; doing A does not guarantee that B is avoided.
predictionHint: Raising the levee is required to avoid flooding, not a guarantee against it.

stimulus: Media critic: Journalists rightly insist that a newspaper's first obligation is to publish what is in the public interest. Yet the same journalists deride papers that devote extensive coverage to the private lives of celebrities. This is inconsistent. Readership surveys consistently show that stories about celebrities' private lives are among those the public is most interested in reading. Extensive celebrity coverage therefore fulfills, rather than betrays, a newspaper's first obligation.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument's reasoning?

choices.A: It assumes that readership surveys accurately measure what readers are interested in.
choices.B: It allows a key phrase to shift in meaning between the statement of the journalists' principle and the conclusion drawn from it.
choices.C: It infers that journalists are inconsistent from the fact that they hold two positions that merely appear to conflict.
choices.D: It takes for granted that whatever the public most wants to read about is something that the public ought to be reading about.
choices.E: It fails to consider that a newspaper may have obligations other than its first obligation.

explanations.A: Wrong force: doubting the surveys attacks a premise; even perfectly accurate surveys would leave the shift in meaning intact.
explanations.B: Correct. 'In the public interest' in the journalists' principle means beneficial to the public; 'the public is most interested in' means popular with readers. The conclusion treats the second as if it satisfied the first.
explanations.C: Half right: the charge of inconsistency is indeed unfounded, but this choice only restates that it is; it does not identify why, which is the equivocation.
explanations.D: Shell game: the argument never claims the public 'ought to' read anything; it moves from what the public is interested in to what is in its interest, which is a different step.
explanations.E: True but irrelevant: the argument concerns only the 'first obligation,' and other obligations do not affect whether that one is met.

keyTakeaway: 'Interesting to the public' and 'in the public interest' are different concepts that share words.
predictionHint: Equivocation on 'public interest.'

stimulus: Toxicologist: Residents living near the Corwin chemical plant report a markedly higher incidence of severe headaches than residents of comparable neighborhoods elsewhere in the city. However, the only substance the plant releases is a compound for which no plausible biological mechanism of producing headaches has ever been proposed. The headaches reported by the residents therefore cannot be caused by anything the plant releases.
stem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: treats the absence of a known explanation for how something could occur as evidence that it does not occur
choices.B: fails to consider that severe headaches may have many causes unrelated to industrial pollution
choices.C: overlooks the possibility that the plant releases substances in quantities too small to be detected
choices.D: relies on a comparison with neighborhoods that may differ from the plant's neighborhood in ways other than proximity to the plant
choices.E: generalizes from the residents of a single neighborhood to the population of the city as a whole

explanations.A: Correct. That no mechanism 'has ever been proposed' shows only that scientists have not yet explained how the compound might cause headaches, not that it does not. Many effects were observed long before their mechanisms were understood.
explanations.B: Opposite: other possible causes would support the toxicologist's denial, not expose a weakness in it.
explanations.C: Premise booster: the stimulus says the compound is 'the only substance the plant releases,' so undetected substances are ruled out by the premises.
explanations.D: Wrong part: doubting the comparison would undermine the correlation itself, which the toxicologist concedes; it does not describe the error in the inference drawn.
explanations.E: Wrong part: the conclusion is confined to 'the residents' near the plant; nothing is claimed about the city as a whole.

keyTakeaway: Not knowing how something could happen is not evidence that it does not happen.
predictionHint: No known mechanism is treated as proof of no effect.

stimulus: Editorial: Supporters of the proposed storm-surge barrier claim that it would substantially reduce the damage that coastal storms inflict on the harbor district. But even the barrier's engineers concede that in a storm of unprecedented severity, water would overtop the barrier and flood the district. A barrier that cannot keep the district dry in every storm offers only an illusion of protection, and the claims of its supporters are therefore unfounded.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: assumes that the barrier's engineers are the most reliable source of information about its performance
choices.B: presumes that a storm of unprecedented severity is likely to occur within the lifetime of the barrier
choices.C: fails to consider that the harbor district might be protected by means other than a barrier
choices.D: criticizes a proposal for failing to achieve a result that its supporters did not claim it would achieve
choices.E: treats the fact that a proposal has a limitation as sufficient reason to reject every argument in its favor

explanations.A: Wrong force: the engineers' concession is used against the barrier, and questioning their reliability would not repair the editorial's inference in any case.
explanations.B: Wrong part: the editorial does not rely on such a storm being likely; its error is in the standard it applies, not in any probability claim.
explanations.C: Out of scope: alternative protections have no bearing on whether the supporters' actual claim has been refuted.
explanations.D: Correct. The supporters claimed the barrier would 'substantially reduce' damage. The editorial refutes a different claim, that it would 'keep the district dry in every storm,' and then declares the original claim unfounded. The target has been quietly upgraded.
explanations.E: Half right: the editorial does over-reject, but 'every argument in its favor' overstates what it does, and this misses that the 'limitation' is not a limitation relative to what was actually claimed.

keyTakeaway: Check the exact claim being refuted against the exact claim that was made; 'reduce' is not 'eliminate.'
predictionHint: Straw man: 'substantially reduce' became 'keep dry in every storm.'

stimulus: Company spokesperson: The consumer agency has charged that our advertisement for the Brisa air purifier misled consumers into believing that the device removes airborne viruses. But the team that produced the advertisement has testified that it never intended to suggest anything about viruses, and internal documents from the campaign's planning confirm that no such suggestion was ever discussed. The agency's charge is therefore baseless.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument's reasoning?

choices.A: It relies on the testimony of the very people whose conduct is being called into question.
choices.B: It assumes that the consumer agency has no evidence beyond the content of the advertisement itself.
choices.C: It fails to consider that the Brisa air purifier may in fact remove airborne viruses.
choices.D: It takes for granted that an advertisement cannot mislead consumers unless it makes an explicit false statement.
choices.E: It treats evidence about what a message was intended to convey as settling what the message actually conveyed.

explanations.A: Wrong force: the testimony is corroborated by 'internal documents,' and even wholly sincere testimony about intent would not answer a charge about effect.
explanations.B: Out of scope: what other evidence the agency holds is never discussed and is not needed to expose the gap.
explanations.C: Opposite: if the device did remove viruses, consumers would not have been misled, which would help the spokesperson rather than reveal a flaw.
explanations.D: Shell game: the argument never invokes explicit false statements; it relies on intent, so this misdescribes the reasoning.
explanations.E: Correct. The charge is that the advertisement 'misled consumers,' a claim about its effect on an audience. Evidence that the makers 'never intended' such a suggestion leaves open whether consumers nonetheless drew it.

keyTakeaway: What a speaker meant and what an audience understood are separate questions; intent does not settle effect.
predictionHint: Intent versus effect: not meaning to mislead is not the same as not misleading.

stimulus: Health columnist: A large randomized study has found that patients who undergo the new laser procedure for correcting nearsightedness are twice as likely to experience a serious complication as patients who undergo the conventional procedure. Twice the risk of serious complication is an alarming difference. Anyone considering the laser procedure should therefore recognize that it is a dangerous one and opt for the conventional procedure instead.
stem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: takes for granted that patients value the avoidance of complications more than they value the benefits of the procedure
choices.B: overlooks the possibility that the conventional procedure has risks of a kind not measured by the study
choices.C: treats a claim about how one risk compares to another as if it established that the risk is large in absolute terms
choices.D: fails to consider that the patients who chose the laser procedure may have been more prone to complications to begin with
choices.E: relies on a single study rather than on a review of all the available evidence

explanations.A: Out of scope: the argument's central claim is that the procedure 'is a dangerous one,' and this choice concerns a value trade-off the argument never makes.
explanations.B: Wrong part: unmeasured risks of the conventional procedure might affect the final recommendation but do not address why 'dangerous' was inferred.
explanations.C: Correct. 'Twice as likely' is a ratio. If the conventional procedure's complication rate is one in ten thousand, the laser procedure's is two in ten thousand, which hardly makes it 'dangerous.' A relative risk says nothing about the absolute level.
explanations.D: Shell game: the study is described as 'randomized,' which rules out patients choosing their procedure; this names a problem the stimulus has already excluded.
explanations.E: Wrong force: the argument's problem is how it reads the study's result, not how many studies it cites.

keyTakeaway: A doubled risk can still be tiny; relative comparisons do not establish absolute magnitude.
predictionHint: Relative versus absolute: twice a small risk is still small.

stimulus: Agricultural economist: In the 1950s, the national grain reserve successfully stabilized bread prices during two consecutive years of poor harvests, releasing stored grain whenever prices began to rise. Bread prices have again become volatile, and critics of the reserve argue that it is no longer needed. They are mistaken: since the reserve stabilized prices before, maintaining it at its 1950s level will stabilize prices now.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: fails to consider that the critics may have reasons for opposing the reserve other than doubts about its effectiveness
choices.B: takes for granted that stabilizing bread prices is a more important goal than reducing the cost of maintaining the reserve
choices.C: infers that the reserve caused prices to stabilize in the 1950s merely because prices stabilized after grain was released
choices.D: presumes, without justification, that a measure that was effective under certain conditions will be effective under conditions that may differ significantly
choices.E: overlooks the possibility that the reserve's release of grain in the 1950s was followed several years later by a period of sharply rising prices

explanations.A: Out of scope: the economist's conclusion is about whether the reserve will work, and the critics' other reasons do not bear on that inference.
explanations.B: Out of scope: no cost comparison is made or needed; the conclusion is about effectiveness.
explanations.C: Premise booster: the stimulus states that the reserve 'successfully stabilized' prices, so the causal claim about the 1950s is a given premise, not a post hoc inference.
explanations.D: Correct. The 1950s success occurred under conditions of poor harvests; today's volatility may stem from different causes, and the market, population, and trade may have changed. A reserve 'at its 1950s level' need not have the same effect now.
explanations.E: True but irrelevant: what happened years after the 1950s release does not affect whether the 1950s success can be projected onto today.

keyTakeaway: A remedy that worked once is evidence only for conditions like those in which it worked.
predictionHint: Different conditions now: the 1950s success may not transfer.

stimulus: Most of the senior partners at the law firm of Greer and Tull attended Hallam Law School, and every attorney who attended Hallam passed the bar examination on the first attempt. It follows that most of the firm's attorneys who passed the bar examination on their first attempt are senior partners.
stem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: infers from the fact that most of one group belong to a second group that most of the second group belong to the first
choices.B: takes for granted that every attorney who passed the bar examination on the first attempt attended Hallam
choices.C: takes for granted that attorneys who attended Hallam are more capable than attorneys who attended other law schools
choices.D: overlooks the possibility that some senior partners did not attend Hallam
choices.E: draws a conclusion about the majority of a group on the basis of premises that provide information about only some members of that group

explanations.A: Correct. The premises establish that most senior partners are first-attempt passers. But the firm may have many junior attorneys who also passed on the first attempt, in which case senior partners could be a small minority of that group. 'Most A are B' does not give 'most B are A.'
explanations.B: Reversal: the argument never needs this converse, and even if every first-attempt passer attended Hallam, junior Hallam graduates could still outnumber the senior partners.
explanations.C: Out of scope: capability plays no role in the argument.
explanations.D: Premise booster: the premise says 'most,' not all, senior partners attended Hallam, so the argument already allows for this.
explanations.E: Wrong force: the premises use 'most' and 'every,' not 'some'; this misstates the quantifiers that are actually in play.

keyTakeaway: 'Most' statements do not reverse; most A being B says nothing about what share of B is A.
predictionHint: Illicit reversal of 'most': junior attorneys may dominate the first-attempt passers.

stimulus: Traffic safety official: Twenty years ago, drivers over the age of seventy were involved in 6 percent of the collisions reported in this province. Last year, they were involved in 11 percent. Since the proportion of collisions involving older drivers has nearly doubled, older drivers today must be considerably more dangerous behind the wheel than older drivers were twenty years ago, and the province should require them to retake the driving test every two years.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument's reasoning?

choices.A: It fails to consider that collisions may be reported more frequently now than they were twenty years ago.
choices.B: It confuses the number of collisions involving older drivers with the proportion of all collisions that involve older drivers.
choices.C: It presumes that older drivers were at fault in the collisions in which they were involved.
choices.D: It takes for granted that requiring older drivers to retake the driving test would reduce the number of collisions.
choices.E: It overlooks the possibility that the share of the province's drivers who are over seventy has grown over the twenty-year period.

explanations.A: True but irrelevant: a change in reporting rates would affect collisions involving drivers of all ages alike and would not alter older drivers' share.
explanations.B: Shell game: the argument speaks consistently of proportions ('6 percent,' '11 percent') and never slips into raw numbers.
explanations.C: Half right: involvement and fault do differ, but the conclusion compares older drivers now with older drivers then, and the involvement-fault gap would have to have changed over time to matter.
explanations.D: Wrong part: this targets the recommendation, but the central inference, that older drivers 'must be considerably more dangerous,' fails before the recommendation is reached.
explanations.E: Correct. If drivers over seventy made up 6 percent of all drivers twenty years ago and 11 percent today, their share of collisions would nearly double even if each older driver were exactly as safe as before. A group's share of an outcome tracks its share of the population.

keyTakeaway: A group's rising share of bad outcomes may only reflect its rising share of the population; look for a per-person rate.
predictionHint: Share of collisions rose because the share of older drivers rose.

stimulus: Consultant: Critics allege that Dunbar Industries pays its employees less than its competitor Searle Manufacturing does. The allegation is baseless. Dunbar and Searle each have the same four departments, and in every one of those departments the average salary of Dunbar's employees is higher than the average salary of Searle's employees in the corresponding department. Therefore, the average salary of Dunbar's employees overall is higher than that of Searle's employees overall.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: relies on average salaries rather than on the salaries actually paid to individual employees
choices.B: takes for granted that the critics' allegation concerns average salaries rather than the salaries of the lowest-paid employees
choices.C: overlooks the possibility that Searle offers its employees benefits that compensate for lower salaries
choices.D: fails to consider that the two companies may differ in the proportion of their employees who work in each department
choices.E: presumes that a comparison that holds for each department at one time will continue to hold in the future

explanations.A: Wrong force: averages are the appropriate measure for the claim being made; individual salaries would not change the structure of the inference.
explanations.B: Shell game: how the critics' allegation should be read is a side issue; the consultant's own inference from departmental averages to the overall average is what fails.
explanations.C: Out of scope: benefits are never at issue; both the allegation and the conclusion concern pay.
explanations.D: Correct. If Searle's workforce is concentrated in its highest-paying department and Dunbar's in its lowest-paying one, Searle's overall average can exceed Dunbar's even though Dunbar wins every department-by-department comparison. The whole is a weighted combination of the parts.
explanations.E: Wrong part: the argument makes no claim about the future; both premise and conclusion are about current salaries.

keyTakeaway: Winning every subgroup comparison does not guarantee winning the overall comparison when the subgroups are weighted differently.
predictionHint: Weighting: departmental averages do not combine into an overall average without headcounts.

stimulus: Agronomist: Some beekeepers blame the new orchard fungicide Veridan for the recent decline in honeybee colonies in the valley, since the decline began shortly after orchards there started using it. But colonies in the neighboring Toll Valley, where no orchards have ever used Veridan, have declined over the same period by nearly the same proportion. The fungicide therefore cannot be responsible for the decline in the valley's honeybee colonies.
stem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.A: takes the occurrence of an effect where a suspected cause is absent as showing that the suspected cause does not contribute to the effect
choices.B: presumes that the honeybee colonies in the two valleys were equally healthy before the decline began
choices.C: takes for granted that wherever Veridan is used, honeybee colonies will decline
choices.D: treats the fact that the decline in the valley began shortly after Veridan was introduced there as evidence that Veridan caused that decline
choices.E: overlooks the possibility that Veridan has harmed insect species other than honeybees

explanations.A: Correct. The Toll Valley decline shows only that something other than Veridan can cause colonies to decline. It does not show that Veridan is not contributing in the valley where it is used; two different causes can produce similar declines in two places.
explanations.B: Out of scope: the argument compares rates of decline, and nothing in it depends on the colonies' prior health.
explanations.C: Reversal: the argument's hidden assumption is that the decline requires Veridan (that Veridan is necessary), not that Veridan always produces decline (that it is sufficient). This names the wrong direction.
explanations.D: Opposite: that is the beekeepers' reasoning, which the agronomist rejects; it is not a flaw in the agronomist's argument.
explanations.E: Out of scope: effects on other insects have no bearing on whether Veridan caused the honeybee decline.

keyTakeaway: An effect appearing without a suspected cause shows the cause is not necessary for the effect, not that it never produces it.
predictionHint: Toll Valley's decline has another cause; that does not clear Veridan.

stimulus: Consumer researcher: In our study, participants who were randomly assigned to read the warning label on the pesticide container before using the product were significantly more likely to handle it safely than participants who were not. Pesticide manufacturers who make warning labels more prominent, so that nearly all users read them, can therefore expect that most users of their products will handle them safely.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument's reasoning?

choices.A: It overlooks the possibility that participants who read the label were already more careful in general than those who did not read it.
choices.B: It takes a difference between two groups in the likelihood of an outcome as establishing that the outcome is likely within one of those groups.
choices.C: It presumes that making a label more prominent will cause users to read it.
choices.D: It generalizes from the handling of a single pesticide to the handling of products of all kinds.
choices.E: It fails to consider that reading a warning label is more likely to produce safe handling when the label is clearly written.

explanations.A: Shell game: participants were 'randomly assigned' to read the label, so pre-existing carefulness was balanced across groups; this names a problem the design has already excluded.
explanations.B: Correct. 'More likely' is comparative. If 10 percent of non-readers and 25 percent of readers handled the pesticide safely, readers are far more likely to be safe, yet most readers are not. The conclusion that 'most users' will be safe needs an absolute figure the study does not supply.
explanations.C: Premise booster: the conclusion is conditioned on labels being made prominent 'so that nearly all users read them,' so this is stipulated.
explanations.D: Wrong part: the conclusion is addressed to 'pesticide manufacturers' about 'their products,' so no leap to products of all kinds is made.
explanations.E: Out of scope: label clarity is never discussed and does not affect the move from 'more likely' to 'most.'

keyTakeaway: 'More likely than' compares two rates; it never tells you whether either rate is above 50 percent.
predictionHint: Comparative to absolute: 'more likely to' is not 'most will.'

stimulus: Novelist: Reviewers of my latest novel complained that its dialogue was stilted and unrealistic throughout. Yet reviewers of the same novel also praised its dialogue as natural-sounding throughout, indeed as the most natural to appear in recent fiction. Since reviewers both condemned and praised the very same dialogue, it is clear that the judgments of the novel's reviewers are self-contradictory.
stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: fails to consider that dialogue can be stilted in some passages of a novel and natural in others
choices.B: presumes that a judgment about a novel's dialogue cannot be both accurate and unfavorable
choices.C: takes for granted that reviewers who praised the dialogue had read the novel more carefully than those who complained
choices.D: relies on the reviews of a single novel to draw a conclusion about the reliability of reviewers in general
choices.E: treats judgments made by different individuals as though they were the judgments of a single individual

explanations.A: Premise booster: both the complaint and the praise are stated to apply 'throughout,' so the passages explanation is excluded by the stimulus.
explanations.B: Out of scope: the argument says nothing about whether the unfavorable judgment was accurate.
explanations.C: Out of scope: the novelist makes no claim about which reviewers read more carefully.
explanations.D: Wrong part: the conclusion is confined to 'the novel's reviewers,' not reviewers in general.
explanations.E: Correct. A judgment is self-contradictory only if one judge holds both halves. If some reviewers found the dialogue stilted and others found it natural, that is disagreement among people, not contradiction within anyone's judgment. 'Reviewers' names a group, not a person.

keyTakeaway: Opposed views held by different members of a group are disagreement, not self-contradiction.
predictionHint: Different reviewers said different things; no single reviewer contradicted himself.

stimulus: Police chief: Eighteen months ago, the city replaced the dim streetlights in the Fairmont district with much brighter ones. Since then, the number of nighttime burglaries reported in Fairmont has fallen by nearly a quarter. The brighter lighting has clearly deterred burglars, and the city should therefore install similar lighting in its other districts.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: The brighter streetlights consume more electricity than the dim ones they replaced.
choices.B: Shortly after the new lights were installed, the police department doubled its nighttime patrols in Fairmont.
choices.C: Some residents of Fairmont have complained that the brighter lights make it difficult to sleep.
choices.D: The number of daytime burglaries reported in Fairmont has remained unchanged over the past eighteen months.
choices.E: Several other cities have also replaced dim streetlights with brighter ones in recent years.

explanations.A: True but irrelevant: electricity cost bears on whether the lights are worth it, not on whether they 'deterred burglars.'
explanations.B: Correct. Doubled patrols during the same period are an alternative explanation for the drop in nighttime burglaries, so the decline cannot be attributed to the lighting.
explanations.C: Out of scope: residents' sleep has nothing to do with the causal claim about burglaries.
explanations.D: Opposite: an unchanged daytime rate alongside a falling nighttime rate suggests that something nighttime-specific, such as lighting, is at work; this supports the chief.
explanations.E: Out of scope: what other cities have done says nothing about what caused Fairmont's decline.

keyTakeaway: When 'Y fell after X,' look for anything else that changed in the same window.
predictionHint: Alternative cause: something besides the lights changed in Fairmont.

stimulus: City official: A survey conducted last month shows that 74 percent of the city's residents favor using public funds to build a new arena for the city's professional hockey team. Since the arena would cost each household only a modest amount in additional taxes, the council should approve the funding; doing so would simply be carrying out the wishes of the city's residents.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: The survey was distributed only to people who had purchased tickets to a hockey game during the past season.
choices.B: A new arena would also be used for concerts and other events that do not involve the hockey team.
choices.C: The additional taxes needed to pay for the arena would be collected over a period of twenty years.
choices.D: Residents of a neighboring city voted five years ago against using public funds to build a similar arena for their own team.
choices.E: Some of the residents surveyed said they would favor the arena only if it were built downtown.

explanations.A: Correct. Ticket buyers are precisely the people most likely to want an arena. A survey confined to them cannot show what 'the city's residents' want, so the claim that funding would carry out residents' wishes collapses.
explanations.B: Out of scope: additional uses might make the arena more attractive but do not bear on whether residents actually support it.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: the payment schedule does not affect what residents want or whether the survey measured it.
explanations.D: Out of scope: a different city's vote tells us nothing about this city's residents.
explanations.E: Wrong force: 'some' residents attaching a condition leaves the 74 percent figure essentially intact.

keyTakeaway: To weaken a survey-based claim, show that the people surveyed are not the people the conclusion is about.
predictionHint: Biased sample: who was actually surveyed?

stimulus: Transportation planner: Traffic on the Route 9 corridor is badly congested during rush hour, with average speeds falling below twenty kilometers per hour. Adding a third lane in each direction would increase the corridor's capacity by 50 percent. The regional authority should therefore widen Route 9, since doing so would relieve rush-hour congestion on the corridor.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: Widening Route 9 would require the regional authority to purchase land from several dozen property owners along the corridor.
choices.B: Average rush-hour speeds on Route 9 were even lower five years ago than they are today.
choices.C: Most of the vehicles on Route 9 during rush hour carry only a single occupant.
