choices.D: When a congested highway is widened, drivers who had been using other routes or traveling at other times soon shift to it.
choices.E: A third lane in each direction would increase the corridor's capacity by somewhat less than 50 percent.

explanations.A: Out of scope: land acquisition is a cost of the plan, not a reason to doubt that it would 'relieve rush-hour congestion.'
explanations.B: True but irrelevant: past speeds do not bear on whether widening would reduce current congestion.
explanations.C: Out of scope: occupancy might suggest a different remedy but does not show that widening would fail.
explanations.D: Correct. If new capacity attracts drivers who currently avoid the corridor, the added lanes fill up and rush-hour congestion persists. The plan would not achieve its stated goal.
explanations.E: Wrong force: 'somewhat less than 50 percent' is still a large capacity increase and would still be expected to relieve congestion.

keyTakeaway: A plan is weakened by showing that the system will respond in a way that defeats the plan's goal.
predictionHint: Induced demand: more lanes attract more drivers.

stimulus: Agronomist: A new variety of drought-tolerant wheat has doubled yields on the arid plains of Keshan over the past three growing seasons. The highlands of neighboring Orvia also suffer from frequent drought, and Orvian farmers struggle with low wheat yields. Introducing the new variety in Orvia would therefore substantially increase the wheat yields of Orvian farmers.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: The new variety of wheat was developed by researchers at an agricultural institute in Keshan.
choices.B: The new variety of wheat fails to mature during the short, cool growing season of highland regions such as Orvia's.
choices.C: Wheat yields in Keshan were already somewhat higher than those in Orvia even before the new variety was introduced there.
choices.D: Orvian farmers grow several crops in addition to wheat.
choices.E: The new variety of wheat produces grain that is somewhat lower in protein than that of traditional varieties.

explanations.A: Out of scope: where the variety was developed has no bearing on whether it would thrive in Orvia.
explanations.B: Correct. The analogy rests on drought being the shared problem. If Orvia's 'highlands' have a short, cool season in which the variety cannot mature, the relevant difference between the two regions defeats the comparison.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: a pre-existing gap in yields does not affect whether the new variety would raise Orvia's yields.
explanations.D: Out of scope: other crops have nothing to do with wheat yields.
explanations.E: Shell game: protein content concerns grain quality, while the conclusion concerns yield.

keyTakeaway: To weaken an analogy, find a difference between the two cases that matters for the outcome predicted.
predictionHint: Relevant difference: highlands are not arid plains.

stimulus: Management consultant: A study of two hundred project teams found that teams whose managers hold frequent meetings experience significantly more interpersonal conflict than teams whose managers hold meetings only occasionally. Frequent meetings evidently generate friction among team members. Managers who want to reduce conflict on their teams should therefore hold meetings less often.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: Team members generally prefer short meetings to long ones.
choices.B: Some of the teams in the study worked on projects that lasted less than one month.
choices.C: Teams whose managers hold frequent meetings complete their projects on time more often than other teams.
choices.D: Interpersonal conflict on project teams is often caused by unclear assignment of responsibilities.
choices.E: Managers typically schedule additional meetings in response to conflicts that have already arisen among team members.

explanations.A: Out of scope: meeting length is never at issue; the argument concerns frequency and conflict.
explanations.B: True but irrelevant: project duration does not affect the relationship between meeting frequency and conflict.
explanations.C: Shell game: on-time completion is a different outcome from conflict and does not challenge the causal claim.
explanations.D: Half right: this names another cause of conflict, but it does not explain why frequent-meeting teams in particular have more conflict, so the correlation remains unexplained.
explanations.E: Correct. If conflict prompts managers to call more meetings, then conflict causes frequent meetings rather than the reverse, and holding fewer meetings would not reduce conflict.

keyTakeaway: Ask whether the supposed effect could be producing the supposed cause.
predictionHint: Reverse causation: conflict leads to meetings.

stimulus: Local historian: County records show that every bridge built in this county before 1900 was constructed with iron trusses, because steel was not available locally until that year. The Miller's Creek bridge, whose construction date is unrecorded, has iron trusses. It was therefore almost certainly built before 1900.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the historian's conclusion?

choices.A: Several bridges in the county that were built before 1900 have since been replaced.
choices.B: The county records from before 1900 are known to be incomplete and do not list every bridge that was built in the county.
choices.C: Because iron remained considerably cheaper than steel, iron trusses continued to be used for small bridges in the county until about 1930.
choices.D: The Miller's Creek bridge was extensively repaired in the 1950s using steel components.
choices.E: Steel trusses are stronger than iron trusses of the same size.

explanations.A: Out of scope: the fate of other bridges has nothing to do with when this one was built.
explanations.B: Wrong part: incomplete records might cast doubt on the premise that every pre-1900 bridge used iron, but the conclusion depends on whether post-1900 bridges also used iron, which this does not address.
explanations.C: Correct. The historian needs iron trusses to indicate a pre-1900 date, but if iron continued in use for three more decades, an iron-truss bridge could easily date from 1900 to 1930. The conditional runs only one way.
explanations.D: True but irrelevant: later repairs do not change the material of the original trusses or when they were built.
explanations.E: Out of scope: relative strength says nothing about when either material was used.

keyTakeaway: 'All pre-1900 bridges are iron' does not mean 'all iron bridges are pre-1900'; weaken by showing the trait persisted.
predictionHint: Show that iron trusses were also used after 1900.

stimulus: Human resources director: Absenteeism at our packaging plant has risen sharply over the past year, forcing us to pay large amounts of overtime to cover for absent workers. To address this, we will begin paying a substantial bonus to every worker who completes a quarter without missing a single shift. Since workers will not want to forfeit the bonus, absenteeism, and with it our overtime costs, will decline.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: Some workers at the plant have never missed a shift and would receive the bonus without changing their behavior.
choices.B: The bonus would cost the plant more than it currently pays in overtime.
choices.C: Workers at a nearby plant that offers no attendance bonus have a lower rate of absenteeism.
choices.D: Most absences at the plant are caused by contagious illnesses that spread quickly when infected workers report for their shifts.
choices.E: The plant's overtime rate is one and a half times the regular hourly wage.

explanations.A: Wrong force: paying some workers who were already present costs money but does not prevent absenteeism from declining among the rest.
explanations.B: Shell game: the conclusion is that absenteeism and overtime costs 'will decline,' not that the plant will save money overall; this attacks a claim the director did not make.
explanations.C: Out of scope: another plant's rate, with no information about why it is lower, says nothing about whether this bonus will work here.
explanations.D: Correct. If the bonus induces sick workers to come in, they infect coworkers, and total absences could rise rather than fall. The plan's incentive would undermine its own goal.
explanations.E: True but irrelevant: the overtime rate explains why overtime is costly but has no bearing on whether absenteeism will decline.

keyTakeaway: A plan is weakened when the behavior it rewards produces the very problem it targets.
predictionHint: Overlooked consequence: rewarding attendance brings sick workers in.

stimulus: City maintenance supervisor: Three years ago we applied a protective coating to the concrete retaining walls along the riverfront, and since then graffiti has been removed from those walls easily and without damage. The historic brick facade of the Caldwell Building has been repeatedly defaced with graffiti. Applying the same coating to the facade would therefore allow graffiti to be removed from it just as easily.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: The coating, once applied, must be reapplied every five years to remain effective.
choices.B: Graffiti has appeared on the riverfront retaining walls less frequently since the coating was applied.
choices.C: Removing graffiti from the Caldwell Building's facade currently requires the use of abrasive techniques that damage the brick.
choices.D: The Caldwell Building's facade is defaced with graffiti more often than the retaining walls are.
choices.E: The coating forms an effective barrier only on dense, nonporous surfaces, and the facade's century-old brick is highly porous.

explanations.A: Out of scope: a maintenance schedule does not affect whether the coating would work on brick.
explanations.B: Out of scope: how often graffiti appears is a different matter from how easily it can be removed.
explanations.C: Opposite: the difficulty of current removal makes the coating more desirable; it gives no reason to think the coating would fail.
explanations.D: True but irrelevant: frequency of defacement does not bear on ease of removal once the coating is applied.
explanations.E: Correct. The analogy from concrete to brick depends on the coating performing the same way on both. If it works only on nonporous surfaces and the brick is porous, the relevant difference breaks the comparison.

keyTakeaway: An analogy between two materials or cases is only as strong as their similarity in the respect that matters.
predictionHint: Relevant difference: brick is not concrete.

stimulus: Economist: A recent poll of small-business owners in the province found that 61 percent plan to hire additional employees within the next six months. Since small businesses account for the majority of the province's private-sector jobs, we can expect a significant rise in private-sector employment in the province over the coming half year.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: Fewer than one in five of the owners contacted answered the poll, and those who declined were mostly owners of struggling businesses.
choices.B: Large corporations in the province have announced plans to expand their operations over the next year.
choices.C: Small-business owners in the province are, on average, considerably more optimistic about the economy than are small-business owners in neighboring provinces.
choices.D: Most of the small-business owners polled plan to hire only one additional employee.
choices.E: Many of the province's small businesses operate in the retail sector, where employment fluctuates seasonally.

explanations.A: Correct. If struggling owners, the ones least likely to hire and most likely to lay off, declined to answer, the 61 percent figure overstates hiring plans across small businesses generally, and the forecast loses its basis.
explanations.B: Opposite: corporate expansion would add to private-sector employment, supporting the forecast.
explanations.C: Out of scope: comparison with other provinces says nothing about whether this province's owners will actually hire.
explanations.D: Wrong force: one new employee at most small businesses in a province would still be a large number of jobs; this does not show the rise would be insignificant.
explanations.E: True but irrelevant: seasonal fluctuation is a general fact that does not undercut the poll's result or its link to employment.

keyTakeaway: Low response rates matter when those who do not respond differ systematically from those who do.
predictionHint: Nonresponse bias: who did not answer the poll?

stimulus: Neurologist: In a trial of the new migraine medication Cefalin, participants recorded the number of migraines they experienced during the month before beginning treatment and again during the third month of treatment. On average, participants experienced 35 percent fewer migraines in the third month of treatment than in the month before treatment began. Cefalin is therefore effective in reducing the frequency of migraines.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: Some participants reported mild nausea during the first two weeks of treatment.
choices.B: Participants in the trial ranged in age from nineteen to sixty-four.
choices.C: Participants were admitted to the trial only during a month in which they had experienced an unusually high number of migraines.
choices.D: The frequency of migraines varies considerably from one person to another.
choices.E: Several migraine medications that are already on the market reduce the frequency of migraines by considerably more than 35 percent.

explanations.A: Out of scope: side effects do not bear on whether migraine frequency fell because of the drug.
explanations.B: True but irrelevant: the age range does not affect the before-and-after comparison.
explanations.C: Correct. If the baseline month was unusually bad by design, participants would be expected to have fewer migraines in a later month with or without treatment. The 35 percent drop may be a return to normal, not an effect of Cefalin.
explanations.D: Wrong force: variation between people does not matter in a design that compares each participant with himself or herself.
explanations.E: Comparison shift: the conclusion is that Cefalin is 'effective,' not that it is the most effective; other drugs' performance is beside the point.

keyTakeaway: A before-and-after improvement is suspect when subjects were selected at their worst.
predictionHint: Regression to the mean: the baseline month was unusually bad.

stimulus: Wildlife official: Five years ago, the Mbeya Reserve began deploying armed anti-poaching patrols. Since then, the reserve's elephant population has grown by 40 percent. The patrols have clearly been effective in protecting the reserve's elephants from poachers, and the government should fund similar patrols in the country's other reserves.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: The anti-poaching patrols in the Mbeya Reserve cost considerably more each year than was originally budgeted for them.
choices.B: Poachers who were active in the Mbeya Reserve five years ago have been arrested in other parts of the country.
choices.C: The elephant population of the Mbeya Reserve had declined steadily throughout the ten years before the patrols were first deployed.
choices.D: Over the same five years, elephant populations in the country's reserves without anti-poaching patrols have also grown by about 40 percent.
choices.E: Elephants in the Mbeya Reserve are now more frequently observed near the reserve's boundaries than they were five years ago.

explanations.A: Out of scope: cost overruns do not bear on whether the patrols caused the population growth.
explanations.B: Out of scope: arrests elsewhere neither confirm nor deny that patrols at Mbeya caused the increase.
explanations.C: Opposite: a steady decline that reversed when patrols began supports the official's causal claim.
explanations.D: Correct. If reserves without patrols grew just as much, the growth at Mbeya is explained by whatever is happening nationwide, and the patrols get no credit. The same effect without the supposed cause undercuts the inference.
explanations.E: True but irrelevant: where elephants are seen says nothing about why their numbers grew.

keyTakeaway: A comparison group that got the same result without the treatment is the sharpest weakener of a causal claim.
predictionHint: Effect without the cause: unpatrolled reserves grew too.

stimulus: Conservation official: The Marsden slipper orchid, which grows only in the wetlands of the Tarn River basin, has declined by half over the past decade. Because the orchid's showy flowers make it highly prized by collectors, the wildlife agency is proposing a strict ban on collecting the plant from the wild. If enacted and enforced, the ban will halt the orchid's decline.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: Several other orchid species that grow in the Tarn River basin are not prized by collectors.
choices.B: Collectors who are caught taking the orchid from the wild currently face only small fines.
choices.C: Nearly half of the Tarn basin's wetlands have been drained for agriculture during the decade of the orchid's decline.
choices.D: The orchid's flowers are at their most showy only during a brief period in late spring, when the wetlands are nearly impossible to reach.
choices.E: Some botanical gardens maintain collections of the Marsden slipper orchid.

explanations.A: Out of scope: other species' appeal to collectors tells us nothing about what is driving this orchid's decline.
explanations.B: Opposite: weak current penalties make a strict ban look more promising, not less.
explanations.C: Correct. The plan assumes collecting is the cause of the decline. If half the orchid's only habitat was drained over the same decade, habitat loss is a competing cause that a collecting ban would not touch, so the ban would not halt the decline.
explanations.D: Wrong force: difficulty of access might reduce collecting somewhat, but it does not show that collecting is not the cause or that the ban would fail.
explanations.E: Out of scope: cultivated collections do not affect whether the wild population will keep declining.

keyTakeaway: A remedy aimed at one cause fails if a different cause is doing the damage.
predictionHint: The plan targets collecting, but habitat loss may be the real cause.

stimulus: Urban planner: Among the forty largest cities in the country, those with the most extensive networks of protected bicycle lanes have the fewest cyclist fatalities per kilometer cycled. Protected lanes thus make cycling safer, and cities that want to reduce cyclist fatalities should build more of them.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: Cities that have the most extensive networks of protected bicycle lanes also have many more cyclists on their streets than other large cities do.
choices.B: Building protected bicycle lanes typically requires removing on-street parking, which business owners often oppose.
choices.C: Cyclist fatalities in the forty largest cities have declined overall during the past decade.
choices.D: In most cities, the majority of cyclist fatalities occur at intersections, where protected lanes end.
choices.E: The cities with the most extensive networks of protected lanes have for decades enforced citywide speed limits far lower than those elsewhere.

explanations.A: Shell game: the planner's measure is fatalities 'per kilometer cycled,' which already adjusts for the number of cyclists; more riders do not explain a lower per-kilometer rate.
explanations.B: Out of scope: political obstacles to building lanes do not bear on whether lanes make cycling safer.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: a general decline across all cities does not explain the difference between cities with and without lanes.
explanations.D: Wrong force: this suggests lanes have a limit, but it does not explain away the correlation; lane-rich cities still have the fewest deaths.
explanations.E: Correct. Long-standing low speed limits are an alternative explanation for both the low fatality rate and, plausibly, the city's investment in cycling. The lanes may be a marker of a safety-minded city rather than the cause of its safety.

keyTakeaway: Check what the rate is normalized by before accepting an answer that attacks the denominator.
predictionHint: Third factor: safety-minded cities both build lanes and have slower traffic.

stimulus: School board member: Three years ago, the rural Pinecrest district moved to a four-day school week with longer school days, and its students' scores on the state assessment have risen steadily since. Our district faces the same budget pressures that prompted Pinecrest's change. Adopting a four-day week with longer days here would therefore raise our students' assessment scores as well.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: Pinecrest's students spent most of the fifth weekday in free tutoring funded by a grant unavailable to other districts.
choices.B: Assessment scores in most of the state's rural districts have remained flat over the past three years.
choices.C: Many parents in the board member's district have expressed concern about the difficulty of arranging child care on the fifth weekday.
choices.D: The board member's district has considerably more students than Pinecrest does.
choices.E: Pinecrest's assessment scores before the change were among the lowest in the state.

explanations.A: Correct. If Pinecrest's gains came from grant-funded tutoring on the fifth day, then the four-day schedule itself was not the cause, and a district without that grant cannot expect the same result. Both the causal claim and the analogy fail.
explanations.B: Opposite: flat scores elsewhere make Pinecrest's rise look more like a result of its change, strengthening the argument.
explanations.C: Out of scope: parental concern about child care does not bear on whether scores would rise.
explanations.D: Wrong force: a size difference is a difference, but nothing shows it is relevant to the effect of a four-day week.
explanations.E: Half right: low starting scores hint at room to improve, but a 'steady' three-year rise is not easily dismissed as a statistical bounce, and this does not identify any other cause.

keyTakeaway: When a policy succeeded elsewhere, ask what else came with the policy that will not come with it here.
predictionHint: Relevant difference: Pinecrest had something else that made the difference.

stimulus: Fisheries minister: The cod stocks off our northern coast have been depleted by overfishing. To reduce the catch, the ministry will purchase and permanently retire one-third of the commercial fishing licenses currently held by the fleet. With a third fewer vessels fishing the northern grounds, the total annual catch of cod will fall substantially, allowing the stocks to recover.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: Cod stocks in other regions have recovered within a decade when fishing was curtailed.
choices.B: The purchase of the licenses will cost the ministry more than it has budgeted.
choices.C: Some of the vessel owners whose licenses are retired under the program will seek employment in industries unrelated to fishing.
choices.D: The owners most likely to accept the offer are those whose vessels are the oldest and least productive in the fleet.
choices.E: The total annual catch of cod has already fallen in recent years as the stocks have declined.

explanations.A: Opposite: recovery elsewhere after curtailment supports the minister's expectation.
explanations.B: Out of scope: cost does not bear on whether the catch will fall.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: what retired owners do next has no effect on the catch of the remaining fleet.
explanations.D: Correct. The plan equates a third fewer vessels with a substantially smaller catch. If the vessels retired are the least productive, removing a third of the licenses removes far less than a third of the catch, and the remaining fleet may continue to overfish.
explanations.E: Wrong force: a catch that is already falling because stocks are depleted does not show that the buyback will fail to reduce it further.

keyTakeaway: A plan that counts units (vessels, licenses) is weakened by showing the units are not equal in what matters (catch).
predictionHint: Fewer boats is not fewer fish if the boats that leave caught little.

stimulus: Consumer advocate: Of the complaints about retailers filed with the provincial consumer protection office last year, 70 percent concerned online retailers, even though online retailers account for only about 20 percent of retail sales in the province. Online retailers are therefore far more likely than conventional retailers to treat their customers unfairly.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: Online retailers in the province have grown rapidly over the past several years.
choices.B: Many of the complaints that were filed about online retailers concerned delays in shipping rather than the quality of the goods purchased.
choices.C: Complaints can be filed with the office only through its website, which online shoppers encounter far more often than other shoppers do.
choices.D: Conventional retailers in the province are required to post the office's contact information in their stores.
choices.E: The office received fewer complaints of all kinds last year than it did the year before.

explanations.A: Out of scope: growth does not explain why online retailers' share of complaints exceeds their share of sales.
explanations.B: Shell game: shipping delays are still a way of treating customers unfairly, so the subject of the complaints does not blunt the conclusion.
explanations.C: Correct. If complaints can be filed only online, shoppers who already buy online are far more likely to file them. The 70 percent figure reflects who finds the complaint channel, not who was treated unfairly, so the inference collapses.
explanations.D: Opposite: making the office easier for conventional shoppers to reach would, if anything, inflate complaints against conventional retailers, making the online share more striking.
explanations.E: True but irrelevant: the total number of complaints does not affect the comparison between the two kinds of retailer.

keyTakeaway: A count of reports measures who reports as much as what happened; check the reporting channel.
predictionHint: Reporting bias: the complaint channel favors online shoppers.

stimulus: Archaeologist: The stone statue unearthed at Velmora must have been carved before the adjacent temple was built. The temple's foundation stones were laid directly around the base of the statue in a way that would have been impossible had the statue not already been standing when the foundation was constructed. Since the temple was built in the fourth century, the statue dates from the fourth century or earlier.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the archaeologist's conclusion?

choices.A: The statue is carved from a type of stone that was quarried near Velmora throughout antiquity.
choices.B: The temple's foundation was completely rebuilt in the seventh century after an earthquake destroyed the original structure.
choices.C: Statues of the same style as the Velmora statue have been found at several sites dating from the third century.
choices.D: Inscriptions on the temple's walls were added in the sixth century.
choices.E: The statue's base shows signs of having been recut at some point after the statue was carved.

explanations.A: True but irrelevant: a stone available 'throughout antiquity' is consistent with any date.
explanations.B: Correct. The evidence shows only that the statue predates the foundation stones now in place. If that foundation was rebuilt in the seventh century, the statue need only predate the seventh century, and the fourth-century date no longer follows.
explanations.C: Opposite: third-century parallels support an early date for the statue.
explanations.D: Half right: later work on the temple sounds relevant, but inscriptions on the 'walls' say nothing about when the 'foundation' around the statue was laid.
explanations.E: Shell game: recutting the base after carving does not tell us when the statue was placed relative to the foundation, so it leaves the archaeologist's inference intact.

keyTakeaway: Physical evidence dates the thing it touches; make sure that thing is the one the conclusion is about.
predictionHint: The foundation around the statue may not be the original foundation.

stimulus: Business journalist: Firms that spend heavily on training their employees have markedly lower rates of employee turnover than firms that spend little on training. Training evidently makes employees more loyal, presumably because it signals that the firm values them. Firms struggling with high turnover should therefore increase their spending on training.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: Employees who have received extensive training frequently leave their firms for better-paying positions at competing firms that offer less training.
choices.B: Firms that spend heavily on training also tend to have more formal procedures for evaluating employee performance.
choices.C: Training programs vary widely in quality from one firm to another.
choices.D: Firms generally invest heavily in training only when they expect their employees to remain long enough for the investment to pay off.
choices.E: Some firms with high turnover have recently increased their spending on training.

explanations.A: Half right: this seems to cut against training, but 'frequently' leaving is compatible with the premise that such firms still have lower turnover overall, so it neither explains the correlation nor overturns it.
explanations.B: Out of scope: evaluation procedures are not linked to turnover by anything in the choice.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: variation in quality does not explain why heavy spenders have lower turnover.
explanations.D: Correct. If firms train heavily because they already expect low turnover, then low turnover leads to training rather than the reverse, and a high-turnover firm that spends more on training has no reason to expect its turnover to fall.
explanations.E: Wrong force: without any information about what happened to those firms' turnover, this neither supports nor undermines the recommendation.

keyTakeaway: Firms choose their investments; ask whether the outcome drove the choice rather than the choice driving the outcome.
predictionHint: Reverse causation: expected retention drives training spending.

stimulus: Medical administrator: Hospitals that perform a given complex operation frequently have markedly lower complication rates for that operation than hospitals that perform it rarely. The explanation is clear: surgeons who perform an operation often become more skilled at it. A low-volume hospital that wants to reduce its complication rate for such an operation should therefore perform the operation more frequently.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: High-volume hospitals typically own more advanced surgical equipment, which they purchased with the revenue generated by performing the operation so frequently.
choices.B: Referring physicians send patients to hospitals with the best outcomes, so hospitals typically become high-volume only after achieving low complication rates.
choices.C: Complication rates for complex operations vary considerably from one surgeon to another within the same hospital.
choices.D: Some low-volume hospitals have complication rates as low as those of the best high-volume hospitals.
choices.E: Patients at high-volume hospitals tend to be sicker on average than patients at low-volume hospitals.

explanations.A: Shell game: this looks like an alternative cause, but the equipment was 'purchased with the revenue generated by performing the operation so frequently,' so volume still produces the lower complication rate, just through a different mechanism. The recommendation survives.
explanations.B: Correct. If low complication rates come first and attract volume, the correlation reflects outcomes causing volume rather than volume causing outcomes. A low-volume hospital that simply performs more operations has no reason to expect its complication rate to fall.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: variation among surgeons within a hospital does not bear on the hospital-level relationship between volume and outcomes.
explanations.D: Wrong force: 'some' exceptions are compatible with the 'markedly lower' average rates the premise reports.
explanations.E: Opposite: if high-volume hospitals achieve lower complication rates despite sicker patients, the case for a volume effect is stronger, not weaker.

keyTakeaway: An alternative mechanism that still runs from the same cause does not weaken; a reversed arrow does.
predictionHint: Reverse causation: good outcomes attract volume.

stimulus: Transit director: Replacing our diesel buses with battery-electric buses will reduce the greenhouse gas emissions produced by the agency's operations. Electric buses emit no exhaust at all, and the diesel buses they replace currently account for over 90 percent of the emissions our operations produce. Even allowing for the electricity the new buses will consume, the switch will therefore cut our operational emissions substantially.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: Manufacturing the batteries for electric buses produces more greenhouse gas emissions than manufacturing an entire diesel bus does.
choices.B: Electric buses have a shorter range than diesel buses and must be recharged during the day.
choices.C: The agency's diesel buses are newer and more fuel-efficient than those of most other transit agencies.
choices.D: The agency plans to expand its total bus service by about 15 percent during the same period in which the electric buses are being introduced.
choices.E: The regional grid is coal-fired, and generating the electricity an electric bus uses per kilometer emits more greenhouse gas than a diesel bus's exhaust does.

explanations.A: Shell game: manufacturing emissions are not emissions 'produced by the agency's operations,' which is the only quantity the conclusion is about.
explanations.B: Out of scope: range and recharging schedules affect logistics, not the emissions comparison.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: the diesel buses' efficiency relative to other agencies' does not change the fact that they produce 90 percent of this agency's emissions or how the switch compares.
explanations.D: Half right: expanded service could raise total emissions, but the conclusion is about what 'the switch' does; a larger fleet would emit even more had it stayed diesel.
explanations.E: Correct. The director has 'allowed for' the electricity but assumed it costs less in emissions than diesel exhaust. If generating each bus's electricity emits more than the diesel bus did, the switch raises operational emissions rather than cutting them.

keyTakeaway: Pin down the exact scope of the conclusion ('operational emissions') and reject answers that attack a broader quantity.
predictionHint: The electricity itself may carry more emissions than the diesel it replaces.

stimulus: Economist: In the eighteen countries that granted their central banks formal independence from elected officials during the past three decades, average inflation in the ten years following the reform was less than half what it had been in the ten years preceding it. Granting a central bank independence is thus an effective means of reducing inflation, and countries now struggling with high inflation should adopt the reform.
stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: In most of the eighteen countries, inflation had already been falling sharply for several years when the reform was enacted.
choices.B: Some countries whose central banks have been formally independent for many decades have nonetheless experienced extended periods of high inflation.
choices.C: Central bank independence is more easily established in countries with stable political institutions.
choices.D: In two of the eighteen countries, the reform was accompanied by large reductions in government spending.
choices.E: Average inflation worldwide has fluctuated considerably over the past three decades.

explanations.A: Correct. If inflation was already falling sharply before the reform in most of the countries, the lower post-reform average is the continuation of a trend that predates the supposed cause. The before-and-after comparison then provides no evidence that the reform did anything.
explanations.B: Wrong force: 'some' countries having high-inflation 'periods' despite independence is compatible with the reform tending to reduce inflation.
explanations.C: Half right: this hints at a confounding factor, but it never connects political stability to inflation, so it does not explain the observed drop.
explanations.D: Wrong force: an alternative cause in 'two of the eighteen' countries leaves the pattern in the other sixteen unexplained.
explanations.E: True but irrelevant: general fluctuation, with no direction or timing, does not account for a consistent fall after the reform.

keyTakeaway: A before-and-after comparison is only evidence of causation if the trend was not already under way before the change.
predictionHint: The decline predated the reform.
